note: Hand transcription made on 2026-11-15 from two NASA tools. Since applied to src/data/launch-vehicles.json and trajectories.json; the scripted snapshots in performance-query.json and ../trajbrowser/windows.json (same numbers) are now the reference.

launchVehicles.source: NASA Launch Services Program Launch Vehicle Performance Website, Performance Query, Orbit = High Energy, https://elvperf.ksc.nasa.gov/Pages/Query.aspx
launchVehicles.units: separated spacecraft mass in kg at the given C3 (km2/s2); a vehicle missing at a C3 was not listed by the site at that C3
launchVehicles.groundRules: Site ground rules: 3-sigma reserves, instantaneous launch attempt, 47 in (1194 mm) adapter, launch from CCSFS (KSC for Falcon Heavy).
findings: Our current lv-vulcan-vc4 curve is about 25-35% too low at every C3 (e.g. 5300 kg vs 7140 kg at C3 10).
Our current lv-falcon-heavy curve is within about 3% of the site.
The site lists Falcon 9 with booster recovery only up to C3 = 10, so it cannot be cited for our present mars-2028 (C3 12) trajectory.

trajectories.source: NASA Ames Trajectory Browser, https://trajbrowser.arc.nasa.gov/traj_browser.php (one-way, custom target list, minimise total delta-V, show all trajectories)
trajectories.columns: launch, arrival, duration, injection C3 km2/s2, post-injection delta-V km/s
trajectories.postInjectionDvMeaning: User guide: for planets, the rendezvous delta-V is the burn at a safe distance above the atmosphere that reduces the speed to escape (C3 = 0). Arrival v-infinity therefore = sqrt((v_esc + dv)^2 - v_esc^2); with v_esc at 200 km above Mars (4.885 km/s), 0.85 km/s gives about 3.0 km/s and 1.11 km/s gives about 3.5 km/s.
trajectories.jupiterNote: The database returned no Jupiter rendezvous trajectories; the flyby list gives the launch energy for a direct transfer. Our jupiter-direct-2029 (C3 80, 1000 days) is consistent with the 2028-12-31 rows.
